title: Dinosaur Hall
subtitle: A Mesozoic diorama you can restage by era — Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous — with true-to-scale creatures and a scholarly field guide.
onboarding: How to read this hall: Context = earth-history framing (eras, climates, body plans). Evidence = named taxa, published length estimates, and clear labels when something is not a dinosaur (pterosaurs, mosasaurs).

eras.label: Triassic
eras.summary: After the end-Permian collapse, the first dinosaurs appear on a warmer, drier supercontinent. Early forms are often bipedal and modest in size.

eras.label: Jurassic
eras.summary: Fern forests, giant sauropods, and famous plate-backed herbivores. Dinosaurs dominate land ecosystems worldwide.

eras.label: Cretaceous
eras.summary: Flowering plants spread. Tyrannosaurs, horned dinosaurs, and hadrosaurs thrive until the end-Cretaceous impact winter.

species.notable: One of the earliest well-known dinosaurs — a slender bipedal hunter from Late Triassic North America.
species.misconception: All early dinosaurs were giant monsters.
species.evidence: Coelophysis averaged roughly 2–3 m long and lightly built; mass death assemblages at Ghost Ranch show many individuals of modest size.
species.imageCredit: James St. John · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: A large early sauropodomorph — long neck, bipedal or quadrupedal stance — hinting at later giant plant-eaters.
species.misconception: Sauropods existed from the very first dinosaurs.
species.evidence: True giant sauropods peak later; Plateosaurus is a Triassic precursor with a different body plan than Jurassic titans.

species.notable: An early South American predator from ~230 Ma, close to the dinosaur root.
species.evidence: Herrerasaurus and related taxa show transitional early dinosaur anatomy in the mid–Late Triassic.

species.notable: A massive Late Jurassic sauropod of western North America — long neck, pillar limbs, whip-like tail.
species.misconception: Brontosaurus and Apatosaurus are totally unrelated names with no scientific history.
species.evidence: Apatosaurus was named first; Brontosaurus was long synonymized, then some species were revived as valid — taxonomy, not movie branding.

species.notable: Plates along the back and spiked tail (thagomizer) — an iconic Late Jurassic herbivore.
species.misconception: The plates were armor like a tank.
species.evidence: Plates were likely for display and/or thermoregulation; the tail spikes were the primary defensive weapons.
species.imageCredit: Mike Pennington · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Apex Late Jurassic theropod — blade-like teeth, strong arms, common in Morrison Formation deposits.
species.evidence: Allosaurus hunted Jurassic prey; Tyrannosaurus is ~80 million years later in the Late Cretaceous.

species.notable: Front limbs longer than hind — a giraffe-like browsing stance among Jurassic giants.
species.misconception: All sauropods dragged their tails on the ground.
species.evidence: Trackways and skeletal biomechanics support elevated tails held off the ground in life.
species.imageCredit: Sheeba Samuel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Extremely long, whip-tailed sauropod — among the longest dinosaurs known from complete skeletons.
species.misconception: Longer always means heavier and slower.
species.evidence: Diplodocus was relatively gracile for its length compared with bulkier titanosaurs and brachiosaurids.
species.imageCredit: Creator:Dmitry Bogdanov · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Late Cretaceous apex predator with crushing bite force and reduced forelimbs.
species.misconception: T. rex was a slow scavenger that never hunted.
species.evidence: Bite force, binocular vision, and healed prey injuries support active predation as well as scavenging.
species.imageCredit: Ben Jacobson ( Kranar Drogin ) · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Three-horned face and broad frill — a classic Maastrichtian herbivore of western North America.
species.misconception: The frill was solid bone armor against T. rex bites.
species.evidence: Frills show vascular channels and display-related variation; horns were used in defense and intraspecific combat.

species.notable: Hollow cranial crest — likely a resonating chamber for calls among hadrosaurs.
species.evidence: Hadrosaurs show terrestrial locomotion and plant-processing teeth suited to land vegetation.
species.imageCredit: Marcin Marucha · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Turkey-sized dromaeosaur with a sickle claw — feathered, not human-sized.
species.misconception: Velociraptors were man-sized and scaly like movie villains.
species.evidence: Fossils show ~2 m length, feathers, and a much smaller body than Jurassic Park depictions.
species.imageCredit: Nobu Tamura ( http://spinops.blogspot.com ) · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: Armored osteoderms and a heavy tail club — a tank-like Late Cretaceous herbivore.
species.misconception: Ankylosaurs could roll into a ball like armadillos.
species.evidence: Body plan is sprawling and heavily plated; defense relied on armor and the club, not rolling.

species.notable: A flying reptile of the Late Cretaceous seas — crest, toothless beak, wings of skin.
species.evidence: Pterosaurs are close archosaur relatives but sit outside Dinosauria; dinosaurs are a separate clade on land (and later birds).
species.imageCredit: Unknown author Unknown author · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

species.notable: A giant marine lizard of the Late Cretaceous oceans — flippers, powerful jaws, not a dinosaur.
species.misconception: Sea monsters like Mosasaurus were swimming dinosaurs.
species.evidence: Mosasaurs are squamates (related to monitor lizards), not dinosaurs; they returned to the sea independently.

quiz.question: Which of these lived in the Jurassic alongside Stegosaurus — not with T. rex?
quiz.explain: Allosaurus is a Late Jurassic theropod. T. rex and Triceratops are Maastrichtian (latest Cretaceous).

quiz.question: Which animal is not a dinosaur?
quiz.explain: Pteranodon is a pterosaur — a flying reptile outside Dinosauria.

quiz.question: About how long was a real Velociraptor?
quiz.explain: Velociraptor mongoliensis was roughly 2 m long and feathered — far smaller than movie raptors.

quiz.question: Which marine reptile is a squamate (lizard relative), not a dinosaur?
quiz.explain: Mosasaurs returned to the sea as marine lizards; dinosaurs never included that lineage.

quiz.question: Which era saw the first dinosaurs after the end-Permian recovery?
quiz.explain: Dinosaurs originate in the Triassic; Coelophysis is a classic Late Triassic example.
